Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service New York NY
350 PM EST Sun Nov 22 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Rainfall amounts have been decreased significantly with this
update. The heaviest rainfall will be confined to far eastern 
LI and southeast CT tonight.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Low pressure will pass just east of Long Island tonight,
keeping most of the rain across eastern Long Island and 
southeast CT.

2) A storm system approaching from the south Wednesday night 
into Thursday will likely bring rain, strong easterly winds,
and widespread coastal flooding to the area Thursday into 
Friday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
.KEY MESSAGE 1...
Guidance has shifted to a more eastward low track the last 24h
with low pressure forecast to track just east of Long Island
tonight. This will keep moderate to locally heavy rain across
far eastern LI and southeast CT. Rainfall amounts wilL range
form little to none for NYC and points north and west, to 0.75 
to 1 inch across far eastern areas. There will likely be a sharp
back edge, but some entrance region dynamics could produce some
light rain to the west of the main axis. The rain will fall 
primarily this evening into the early morning hours Monday. In 
addition, with the more eastward track, winds will also be 
substantially weaker.

Any lingering rain will exit eastern areas in the morning with
clearing skies, followed by a cold frontal passage in the 
afternoon. NW winds in the afternoon will gusts to around 20 
mph, with another warm afternoon in the 60s. Most of the record 
highs are around 70. KISP has tied or broken its high
temperature record the last 4 days. It seems unlikely this will
happen on Monday. 

A minimal coastal flood threat at most continues for the south shore 
back bays of Nassau County and Queens during the Monday morning high 
tide cycle. Guidance and recent trends point to a greater 
probability that tide levels fall just short of minor flooding 
benchmarks. Additionally, the progressive nature of the low pressure 
system passing nearby would hamper the opportunity for tidal piling 
leading up to the high tide. As such, there are no plans at this 
time to issue a Coastal Flood Statement for Monday morning.

Much cooler weather will be on tap for Tuesday and Wednesday as
an anomalously (2-3SD+) strong area of high pressure (1040+ mb)
builds to the north. Daytimes high will struggle to get out of 
the 40s with lows manly below freezing except NYC metro 
Wednesday morning.

.KEY MESSAGE 2... 
A much larger scale system will bring potentially significant
impacts to the area late Wednesday night into Friday, with rain,
wind, and widespread coastal flooding. This will be a very
different system than the former with a large frontal zone and 
a west to east area of rain from the Ohio Valley to offshore the
Atlantic seaboard. So any chance of escaping the inclement 
weather for the holiday is unlikely. The question is what will 
be the extent of the impacts. The anomalously strong surface 
high to the north will give way to a broad area of low pressure 
tracking northward along the eastern seaboard. There are some 
solutions that have the low tracking farther west along the 
spine of Appalachians, but regardless a strong pressure gradient
will be in place between the departing high and approaching low
pressure system. Winds will gradually strengthen Wednesday into
THursday, with the strongest winds during the daytime hours 
Thursday. A consensus forecast right now produces ENE winds of 
20 to 30 mph with gusts 35 to 45 mph, possibly even 50 mph at 
the coast. Rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches seem reasonable at 
this time with the progressive nature of the system. In 
addition, with a strong subtrop jet (courtesy of El Nino) these 
southern stream systems are loaded with moisture as they 
interact with mid latitude energy. 

Coastal flooding is also growing more likely with a full moon 
on the 24th and king tides this week. Many locations need less 
than a foot to reach minor coastal flood benchmarks. The way it 
stands, the current forecast supports widespread minor to 
moderate flooding, perhaps even localized major on Thursday. In
addition beach flooding, erosion, and overwash would all be on 
the table.

&&

.AVIATION /21Z SUNDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Weak low pressure will pass off to the south and east tonight. 

KLGA still hanging onto LIFR cigs in persistent ENE flow off
Long Island Sound. Cigs there may improve after 20Z but then 
go back down to LIFR after 00Z. All other terminals except KTEB 
are VFR attm, and cigs should go down through MVFR to IFR this 
evening. Rain now looks to remain well to the east at 
KBDR/KISP/KGON and should be on the light side. Improvement to 
MVFR expected late tonight into early Mon morning, with VFR 
returning during the morning hours. 

E-NE winds 10 kt or less should back N and then NW from late
evening into the overnight, then become W late tonight into 
mid morning Mon. Gusts 15-18 kt may still be possible after 
midnight at KGON. 

 ...NY Metro (KEWR/KLGA/KJFK/KTEB) TAF Uncertainty...

Degree of improvement at KLGA highly uncertain given flow off
the eastern Sound. Some improvement may occur from 20Z-24Z. 

.OUTLOOK FOR 18Z Monday through Thursday... 

Monday afternoon and night: VFR. Cold fropa late in the
afternoon with NW winds with gusts 15-20 kt. 

Tuesday into Tuesday evening: VFR. NW winds 15-20 kt with gusts
20-25 kt. 

Late Tuesday night and Wednesday: VFR. 

Wednesday night: MVFR cigs developing with slight chance of rain 
late. Increasing E-NE winds with gusts 20-30 kt, highest in the 
NYC metro area and along the coast. 

Thursday: Rain with IFR cond. E-NE winds gusting to 35-45 kt,
highest in the NYC metro area and along the coast. 

Friday: Still a chance of rain mainly in the morning, with
flight cat improving to MVFR. W winds gusting to 25-30 kt. 

Detailed information, including hourly TAF wind component
forecasts, can be found at: https:/www.weather.gov/zny/n90

&&

.MARINE...
Gale warning have been dropped on the outer ocean water (20 to
60 nm) due to more eastward track of low pressure tonight. The
nearshore ocean zones remain under a SCA. The only non-ocean
zones to maintain a SCA is LI Sound east of the CT River. This 
is mainly due to large ocean waves and shoaling just east of 
Montauk Point northward into the waters. SCA on the ocean 
waters continues through Monday night due to NW flow in cold 
advection and lingering high seas. 

A brief lull in SCA conditions is possible on the near shore 
ocean waters for Tue afternoon and night before winds and seas 
ramp up on Wed with the approach of low pressure from the S, 
interacting with strong high pressure to the north to produce 
strong E-NE winds. On the ocean, gusts 25-30 kt likely to return
by Wed evening, ramping up to gale force by Wed night and to 
storm force on Thu. Gale force wind gusts should arrive to the 
non ocean waters by late Wed night and continue into Thu. Max 
significant wave heights should ramp up to 15-20 ft on the ocean
and occasionally to 20-25 ft out east, 7-10 ft across LI Sound 
and around 10 ft on western Block Island Sound E of Orient 
Point.
